paper: Anton, Cohen & Quer-Sardanyons (2017/2020) — A fully discrete approximation of the 1D stochastic heat equation (arXiv:1711.08340, IMA J. Numer. Anal.)
domain: SPDE numerics — 1D stochastic heat equation with space-time white noise, explicit stochastic exponential integrator (SEXP), finite-difference space + DST diagonalization
note: These five questions are genuinely OPEN after the present replication. They are not rhetorical: each is stated with its evidentiary basis (what in the report / in the paper triggers the question) and concrete next steps that a follow-up study could take. None of them, individually or jointly, would downgrade the current REPLICATED verdict; they mark the boundary between what was actually verified here and what a stronger replication would test.

questions.q: Is the empirically observed temporal strong order 0.558 the finite-sample estimator of an underlying true rate of exactly 1/2, or does the ~0.06 excess persist under larger sample sizes and finer coarse grids?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §4/C2 reports slope 0.558 over Δt=2^-3..2^-10 at M=512 with Ms=500 samples. This exceeds the paper's stated 1/2 by ~12%. No bootstrap CI on the slope was computed, and the coarsest points (Δt=2^-3, E[sup|·|^2]=2.575) are the noisiest Monte-Carlo estimators in the regression. Under classic strong-order theory for SEXP applied to a globally-Lipschitz semilinear parabolic SPDE with additive-like noise, the theoretical rate is 1/2 in time (Fig-1 style), matching only if the 0.058 excess is MC/regression noise.
next_steps: Rerun the strong-order experiment at Ms ∈ {1000, 2000, 5000} and report slope with a bias-corrected bootstrap 95% CI.
Restrict the regression to Δt=2^-5..2^-10 (drop the two coarsest, high-error points) and recheck the slope.
Repeat at M ∈ {256, 1024} to confirm the slope is M-independent (isolating temporal error).
If the CI covers 1/2, close as 'consistent with 1/2 up to MC noise'; if not, investigate whether the discrete Nemytskii σ(u)=1-u introduces a measurable rate perturbation.

questions.q: Does the proved L^q(Ω) temporal rate 1/4^- (Thm 2.3) actually manifest empirically under joint (Δt, Δx) refinement with the sup-in-(t,x), L^q-in-Ω norm the theorem uses, as opposed to the temporal-only Δx-fixed setup of Fig 1?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §2 (row C5) and §8 explicitly mark Thm 2.3 as 'proof-only, out of scope'; the replication measures only the Fig-1 empirical order 1/2 with M fixed at 512. The gap between the proved 1/4^- (which includes a spatial contribution and uses an L^q(Ω;C([0,T]×[0,1])) norm) and the empirically observed 1/2 (temporal only) is not addressed by this replication.
next_steps: Design a joint-refinement grid: pairs (Δt_k, Δx_k) with Δx_k = c·Δt_k^{1/2} so temporal and spatial contributions scale together in the proof's norm.
Compute the L^q-in-Ω, sup-in-(t,x) error against a doubly-refined reference (M_ref=2048, Δt_ref=2^-18) for q ∈ {2, 4, 8}.
Fit the observed rate; check whether the slope approaches 1/4 as q grows and the coarse pairs shrink.
If the observed rate stays above 1/4 across q and refinement, this is itself an interesting reproducibility observation and should be flagged as such.

questions.q: Which of the two candidate interpretations of the discrete Wiener increment ΔW^n in Eq. (15) — literal ΔW^n ~ N(0, Δt) (which blows up at M=512 for Δt > 2^-10) versus the cell-increment ΔW^n ~ N(0, Δt/M) (which reproduces Fig 1) — did the paper's authors actually implement, and can this be settled from the paper's LaTeX source, code (if any), or direct correspondence?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §5 documents the noise-scaling ambiguity: a literal reading of Σ=√M·σ combined with ΔW^n ~ N(0, Δt) applies √M twice, giving per-node noise √M·σ·√Δt and causing explicit-scheme blowup for Δt > 2^-10 at M=512 (measured max|u| ~ 10^6–10^13). The consistent cell-increment reading (ΔW^n ~ N(0, Δt/M)) cancels the √M and gives σ(u_m)·√Δt·ξ, reproducing CFL-freeness (C1) and Fig-1 order (C2). Our replication picked the physically-standard cell-increment reading and all three judges accepted it, but the paper text itself does not unambiguously state which convention Eq. (15) uses.
next_steps: Re-scan the arXiv LaTeX source (already fetched in work/src/) for the definition of ΔW^n and Σ, including footnotes and Appendix material, to see if the convention is stated more precisely than in the printed body.
Check the paper's own numerical section for any equation that fixes the units of ΔW^n (e.g. a Cov[ΔW^n_m, ΔW^n_m'] expression).
If the authors have released a companion code (Matlab/Julia) — e.g. on a personal page or IMA-JNA supplement — inspect the exact random-increment scaling used.
If nothing definitive is found, contact the corresponding author (Anton or Cohen) with a brief methods clarification query, citing our finding.
Regardless of outcome: document the convention explicitly in any follow-up SPDE numerics paper that cites this scheme.

questions.q: Does the paper's Thm 2.4 almost-sure convergence result actually enforce, for any single realization ω, a rate arbitrarily close to 1/2, or is the per-path rate strictly slower than the moment-in-Ω rate, and what is the correct rate exponent for pathwise convergence of SEXP on this SPDE?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §4/C3 measures per-path slopes {0.568, 0.525, 0.562, 0.547, 0.535} over 5 realizations at M=512, Δt_ref=2^-15 — remarkably close to the moment RMS slope 0.558 of C2. This is empirically clean, but classical SDE theory (Kloeden–Platen) warns that a.s. convergence rates for strong schemes are typically strictly slower than moment rates (by an arbitrarily small ε due to Borel–Cantelli / iterated-logarithm penalties). Thm 2.4 in the paper is stated qualitatively ('almost-sure convergence'), and our empirical per-path rates suggest that in practice the loss vs. the moment rate is negligible for this scheme — but whether this is exact, or whether it degrades at much smaller Δt below the reference resolution, is not resolved.
next_steps: Extend the pathwise experiment to N_paths ∈ {50, 100} and finer reference Δt_ref=2^-18 so a broader range of coarse Δt can be probed.
Fit log-log per-path slopes and compare the empirical distribution mean/median/quantiles to the moment slope from C2.
Test explicit worst-case ω by rejection-sampling paths with unusually large ||W|| and checking whether their per-path slopes remain ≈ 1/2.
Consult the paper's proof of Thm 2.4 to determine whether the stated a.s. convergence carries an explicit rate (e.g. 1/2 - ε for any ε > 0).

questions.q: Does the SEXP scheme's observed 1/2 strong temporal rate and CFL-freeness generalize to non-globally-Lipschitz σ (the Sec-3 regime of Thm 3.1, 'convergence in probability'), or is the rate qualitatively degraded there — and if so, is a modified SEXP (e.g. tamed or truncated Σ) needed to recover order 1/2?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §1 and §2 note that Thm 3.1 is stated for non-globally-Lipschitz coefficients but only proves convergence in probability (weaker than the L^q(Ω) rate of Thm 2.3). The paper does not report an empirical rate for that regime, and this replication used only the globally-Lipschitz test problem σ(u) = 1-u. Recent SPDE literature (Hutzenthaler–Jentzen 2015, Becker–Gess–Jentzen–Kloeden 2020) shows explicit schemes for non-Lipschitz SPDEs can fail to be strongly convergent unless tamed/split-step modifications are used. Whether SEXP as written is genuinely usable in the Sec-3 regime, and at what empirical rate, is an open follow-up.
next_steps: Design a non-Lipschitz test problem within the paper's Thm 3.1 hypotheses (e.g. σ(u)=√(1+u^2) with polynomial growth, or σ(u)=u/(1+u^2)).
Run the same strong-order protocol (M=512, Δt=2^-3..2^-10, Ms=500 with a fine Δt_ref).
Track (a) blow-up frequency across samples, (b) empirical strong order on non-blown-up trajectories, and (c) whether a tamed variant (Σ_tamed = Σ / (1 + Δt·|Σ|)) restores clean order-1/2 behavior.
If SEXP degrades, this identifies an open extension: adapt the tamed-Euler ideas of Hutzenthaler et al. to the SEXP linear-part structure and re-derive the strong rate.
This is potentially publishable in its own right as an extension study.
